cues.text:
Imagine a reviewer opens a training pull
request and sees only the words 'tests
passed.' Which tests, and on what files?

We'll give both agent clients a
convention that answers those questions.

Whenever the quantity validator changes,
the evidence should name the exact test

command, the outcome, and the files
checked.

Those three fields give us a clear pass
condition for this exercise.

Open the project instructions for each
client.

In this lab, Claude Code reads the
convention through Claude dot M D,

and OpenCode reads it through Agents dot
M D.

The files repeat the same short
requirement.

Your installed versions and workspace
settings determine which project

guidance is loaded, so compare the
actual paths before assuming that both
sessions received the convention.

Next, open Skill dot M D. The
description explains when the procedure

is useful: summarizing test evidence for
a training pull request.

The body says which fields to return and
in what format.

If you need a reusable evidence
template, include it with the skill in a
location the client supports.

Keep the first version short so you can
tell which part helped.

From the repository root, follow the
skill path for each client.

Here the paths start with dot Claude and
dot OpenCode.

The base filename is the same: Skill dot
M D.

Compare the file contents with what the
session reports loading and confirm

precedence if more than one definition
exists.

A matching name on disk by itself tells
you where the file is,

so take one more step and test the
behavior.

Start a fresh session in each client and
provide the same recorded run.

Ask for the pull request evidence
summary.

The example returns the command, four
passing tests,

and the validator and zero-boundary test
as the checked scope.

Confirm each item against the captured
run. If the client shows the skill

invocation, note that signal alongside
the behavior you observed.

Try a second prompt: explain how order
IDs are formatted,
and cite the defining file.

The skill's test-evidence output would
add clutter here.

Look for a simple explanation and a path
instead.

This gives you a practical two-case test
for the skill:

one matching request and one unrelated
request.

Keep both examples when you revise the
description.

Notice that the evidence template
includes a test command.

A repository file can describe that
command and the skill can format its
output.

The workspace controls whether the
client may execute it and whether
approval is needed.

Read the proposed command and the actual
policy.

The author can then hand the resulting
evidence to an independent reviewer for
a decision.

Review the persistent instruction files
and the skill files in the repository
diff.

Include the matching and unrelated
results in the pull request,
along with the client versions.

Someone reading that evidence should be
able to reproduce both outcomes.

Then one person can keep the rule
aligned across tools while a separate
reviewer checks what changed.
